question: What is venepuncture primarily used for in clinical practice?
explanation: Venepuncture involves piercing a vein to collect blood samples needed for various laboratory investigations. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is proper technique so important when doing venepuncture?

options.A: To eliminate the need for hand washing
options.B: To reduce the cost of laboratory reagents
options.C: To prevent patient harm and protect sample quality
options.D: To speed up the patient discharge time

explanation: Taking your time to use the right technique keeps your patient safe from injury and ensures the lab gets an accurate, unblemished sample. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h1)

question: Which vein inside the bend of the elbow (antecubital fossa) is usually our first choice for drawing blood?
explanation: The median cubital vein is your best friend in the ward! It sits nicely, doesn't roll around easily, and makes a great target for your needle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why must you be extra careful when trying to use the basilic vein for venepuncture?

options.A: It lies close to the brachial artery and median nerve
options.B: It carries oxygenated blood directly from the lungs
options.C: It is too small to yield an adequate blood sample
options.D: It has thick muscular walls that resist needle entry

explanation: Be cautious with the basilic vein—major nerves and the brachial artery run right beside it, so care is needed to avoid accidental injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h2)

question: In which of these situations should you definitely AVOID drawing blood from that arm?

options.A: A patient with a mild headache
options.B: A fasting patient scheduled for routine labs
options.C: An arm with an active dialysis fistula
options.D: An adult over the age of sixty

explanation: Never touch an arm with an active dialysis fistula! Doing so can damage their vascular access and put the patient in serious danger. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h3)

question: A patient had a right-sided mastectomy last year. Which arm should you use for venepuncture?

options.C: In the right hand veins only

explanation: Always avoid the arm on the side of a previous mastectomy because lymph flow there is compromised, making infections much harder to fight off. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the main reason we tie a tourniquet before doing venepuncture?

options.A: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the hand
options.B: To numb the puncture site and reduce pain
options.C: To disinfect the skin surface before needle entry
options.D: To engorge and make the veins more visible

explanation: The tourniquet gently slows down blood returning to the heart, causing the veins to pop up nicely so they are easier to see and feel. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why do blood collection sample tubes come with different colored tops?

options.A: They contain different chemical additives for specific tests
options.B: They indicate the date the tubes were manufactured
options.C: They show which department ordered the laboratory test
options.D: They represent the different sizes of the patient's veins

explanation: Those color codes are lifesavers! They tell you which additive (like anticoagulants or clot activators) is inside for specific lab investigations. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why must you wait for the skin antiseptic to dry completely before inserting the needle?

options.A: To make the skin tougher so the needle enters smoothly
options.B: To ensure the tourniquet stays firmly in place on the skin
options.C: To prevent the adhesive bandage from sticking too early
options.D: To allow the chemical to kill microorganisms and prevent sample damage

explanation: Patience is key! Giving the antiseptic time to dry lets it kill germs properly and stops wet alcohol from stinging the patient or ruining the blood sample. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which of these actions goes against safe infection control practice during venepuncture?

options.A: Recapping used needles using a two-handed technique
options.B: Disposing of the needle directly into a rigid sharps bin
options.C: Performing hand hygiene before putting on clean gloves
options.D: Cleaning the insertion site in a circular outward motion

explanation: Never use two hands to recap a needle! That is a quick way to get an accidental needlestick injury. Always use one hand or drop it straight into the sharps box. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h5)

question: At what angle should you typically insert the venepuncture needle into the skin?
explanation: A gentle angle of 15 to 30 degrees lets you slide smoothly into the vein without accidentally poking right through the other side! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h6)

question: At what point in the procedure should you release the tourniquet?

options.A: Immediately after the first blood tube is filled
options.B: Before pulling the needle out of the vein
options.C: Before inserting the needle into the skin
options.D: After applying the adhesive bandage to the arm

explanation: Remember to release the tourniquet before taking the needle out. This stops extra blood from leaking out and prevents a nasty bruise from forming. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h6)

question: What does 'sample hemolysis' mean in the laboratory?

options.A: The rupture of red blood cells releasing contents into serum
options.B: The formation of a painful bruise underneath the skin
options.C: The rapid clotting of blood inside the vacuum tube
options.D: The complete absence of blood flow into the collection tube

explanation: Hemolysis happens when delicate red blood cells burst open, coloring the serum pink or red and messing up test results like potassium levels. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is your best first step if a painful bruise (hematoma) starts swelling up while you are trying to find a vein?

options.A: Remove the tourniquet and withdraw the needle at once
options.B: Apply an ice pack directly over the needle while it remains inside
options.C: Push the needle deeper to secure better placement in the vein
options.D: Leave the tourniquet tight and attach a larger vacuum tube

explanation: If a hematoma starts forming, stop right away! Remove the tourniquet and pull out the needle to keep the patient comfortable and prevent more bleeding under the skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why should you tell your patient NOT to bend their elbow right after getting blood drawn?

options.A: It forces the needle site to bleed faster than normal
options.B: It increases the risk of bruising and hematoma formation
options.C: It stops the remaining blood from flowing into the fingers
options.D: It causes the adhesive bandage to fall off the arm

explanation: Bending the arm puts pressure on the fresh puncture spot, which pops the clot loose and causes blood to leak underneath the skin into a nasty bruise. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h8)

question: When is the absolute right time to label your blood collection tubes?

options.A: At the bedside immediately after collection
options.B: At the nurses' station at the end of the shift
options.C: After returning from the hospital laboratory counter
options.D: Before entering the patient's room for the procedure

explanation: Always label your tubes right there at the bedside before you leave the patient. Never wait, because mixing up blood samples can have serious consequences! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h8)
